title: Earth in Motion
theme: Earth science: the slow forces that shape land
objectives: I can use ten earth science words to explain how layers, plates, and cracks change land.
I can tell the difference between an everyday meaning and a science meaning of fault and pressure.
I can explain how sediment becomes rock and how a fossil forms.
I can write a short explanation of a landform using at least four words from this unit.
rationale: Earth science asks sixth graders to explain how very slow processes build very large things, and the explanations depend on exact words. Three tier 3 terms (sediment, tectonic, fossil) anchor the unit, and the tier 2 verbs and nouns (deposit, accumulate, collide, molten, boundary, fault, pressure) are the ones students need to say how and where. Fault and pressure also have everyday meanings, so the unit shows students how a familiar word can carry a technical meaning in science.

passage.title: Reading the Rocks
paras: A rock layer is a diary of the past. Rivers, wind, and waves pick up tiny bits of rock, sand, and mud, and they carry these bits away. When moving water slows down, it begins to deposit that material on the bottom of a lake, river, or sea. The material is called sediment. Year after year, more sediment accumulates on top of the first layer, and the layers pile up like pages in a book.

The weight of the upper layers creates enormous pressure. Over a very long time, that pressure squeezes the lower layers until the loose grains stick together as solid rock. Sometimes a shell, a leaf, or a bone is buried before it can rot away. When the layers harden around it, the buried remains can become a fossil, a trace of ancient life preserved in stone.

How, then, can a fossil of a sea creature end up on a mountain? The answer is tectonic motion. Earth's rocky outer shell is broken into huge pieces called plates, and they slowly move, usually only a few centimeters each year. The place where two plates meet is called a boundary. At some boundaries, plates collide, and the crumpling rock is pushed upward over millions of years. The Himalayas formed this way when two plates collided.

Deep below the surface, some rock is so hot that it becomes molten, which means melted into a thick liquid. At certain plate boundaries, molten rock rises through cracks and erupts from volcanoes. When it cools, it hardens into new rock.

Plates do not always collide head-on. Sometimes they slide past each other, and the rocks along their edges catch and strain. A long crack where blocks of rock have moved is called a fault. When the stuck rock finally slips along a fault, the ground shakes in an earthquake. California's San Andreas Fault is one famous example. Each layer, mountain, and crack is a clue, and together they tell Earth's slow story.

qs.why: More sediment lands on the first layer each year, so the layers build up.

qs.q: Why can a fossil of a sea creature be found on a mountain?
choices: Rock that formed under water was later pushed upward when plates collided.
Sea creatures once climbed the mountains.
Volcanoes carried the animals to the top.
Rivers deposit fossils at the tops of mountains.
qs.why: The passage links plates colliding to crumpled rock pushed upward over millions of years, which lifts old sea-floor layers.

qs.q: Which detail best explains how loose sediment becomes solid rock?
choices: Rivers carry bits of rock away.
The weight of upper layers squeezes the lower layers until the grains stick together.
A shell can be buried before it rots.
Plates move a few centimeters each year.
qs.why: The passage says pressure from the weight above squeezes the lower layers into solid rock.

qs.q: In paragraph 4, what does "molten" tell you about the rock?
choices: It is soft and wet from rain.
qs.why: The paragraph defines molten as melted into a thick liquid and says it comes out of volcanoes.

qs.q: Which statement best expresses a central idea of the passage?
choices: Earthquakes are the most important event in Earth's history.
Fossils can be found only on mountains.
Slow processes such as layering, moving plates, and cracking shape and record Earth's history.
Volcanoes are the cause of every mountain range.
qs.why: The passage connects layering, plates, volcanoes, and faults as slow processes that leave clues in rock.

teacher.overview: Students learn ten earth science words and use them to explain how layers, plates, and cracks shape land. They read a science passage about reading rock layers, study word families, and write explanations that follow a cause-and-effect order.

notes.va.sediment.n: Use a jar of muddy water to show sediment settling. Clarify that sediment is the loose material and sedimentary is the adjective for the rock it makes. Students often use it for any dirt.
notes.va.tectonic.adj: Tectonic is the adjective; plates is the noun it usually describes. Do not worry about the Greek roots at this level. Ask students to say the phrase tectonic plates three times aloud.
notes.va.fossil.n: A fossil is a trace of ancient life, not the animal itself and not any old bone. Use pictures of footprints, leaf prints, and shells in stone. Students may confuse fossil with fossil fuel; name it as a related use.
notes.va.deposit.v: Teach the science sense (drop and leave) first, then the bank sense as a different meaning. Pair with erode: rivers erode in one place and deposit in another. Stress is on the second syllable for the verb.
notes.va.accumulate.v: Accumulate is for slow growth: dust, snow, sediment, points. Contrast with just pile up all at once. Have students list three things that accumulate in their backpacks.
notes.va.collide.v: Collide needs two moving things. Use two toy cars, then two sheets of paper pushed together to model crumpling at a boundary. Link to collision.
notes.va.molten.adj: Molten is only used for things that are usually solid. Contrast with melted ice cream. Ask students why molten is a better word for lava than melted.
notes.va.boundary.n: A boundary is where something ends and something else begins. Use state borders and playground lines first, then plate boundaries. Students often think a boundary is the edge of a map only.
notes.va.fault.n: Teach the science meaning first: a crack in rock where blocks have moved. Name the second meaning (blame) so students notice it in other readings. Show the San Andreas Fault on a map.
notes.va.pressure.n: Pressure is a steady push. Use a hand pressed on a sponge. Name the second meaning: stress or pushing someone to do something. Connect to how weight above creates pressure on the layers below.

teacher.model: Think-aloud: 'The passage says layers of sediment accumulate, and the weight creates pressure. I picture mud piling up on a lake bottom, and the weight squeezing the lower layers. After a long time, the pressure turns the sediment into rock. Each word gives one step in the process.'

teacher.reviewAdvice: Revisit the layer-building words (deposit, accumulate) and the plate words (collide, boundary, fault) two days later by having students order them in a cause-and-effect chain. Connect to erode, gradual, shift, and evolve from the change unit.

wida.oral: Partner A draws a simple diagram of a rock layer or a plate boundary and describes it aloud. Partner B names the unit words they hear and says one cause-and-effect link.

needsReview: Facts in the passage need a science teacher's check: plates usually move a few centimeters per year; the Himalayas formed where two plates collided; molten rock rises at certain plate boundaries and erupts from volcanoes; the San Andreas Fault is in California; fossils of sea creatures occur in rock that was uplifted. Statements are kept general on purpose.
Spanish glosses not reviewed by a native speaker: fundido (molten), límite (boundary), chocar (collide), falla (fault), depositar, acumularse.
Sense boundaries: deposit (money sense named in senses), fault (blame sense named in senses), pressure (stress sense named in senses). Tectonic synonym 'geologic' is broader than tectonic.
The word 'dregs' was left out of the sediment synonyms to keep them grade-appropriate.
